options.label: Sell her to Vell
options.outcome: Vell tucks the jar under his arm like a loaf. Tansy has stopped hammering on the glass. She watches you count the coins, and she does not look away until he has turned the corner.
options.chronicle: Sold a fairy in a jar to Ambrose Vell. Good price. She watched me count it, the whole time.

road.hint: Some prices are paid by whoever is inside the jar.

options.label: Let her go, and sell Vell the dust
options.outcome: You break the wax and she tumbles out, gasping. Vell scrapes the glass into a silk bag with a little silver spoon, pinch by pinch, while she watches from the floor. Her wings are still bent. "That was my flying," she says, and limps off into the dark on foot.
options.chronicle: Freed a fairy and sold her shed dust to Vell. She was free. She said it was her flying. She walked away on foot.

road.hint: What was shed can still belong to the one who shed it.

options.label: Let her go, and give her back the dust
options.outcome: You break the jar and tip the glass toward her. The dust rises off it like frost off a window in the sun and settles back into her wings, and her wings straighten with a sound like a page turning. She loops round your head and kisses your cheek, a warm spot no bigger than a pinprick. Vell closes his purse with a small sigh. It was never dust: it is scales, thousands of them laid like roof slates, the same as on a moth's wing.

delayed.text: A ring of tiny mushrooms has sprung up on the stair. In the middle sits a thimble of something golden.

options.chronicle: Turned down Vell's money for a fairy's shed dust and gave it back to her. It went back into her wings. She flew off over my head.

road.hint: A gift left in a ring of mushrooms comes from someone small with a long memory.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you, Vell picks up the jar.
options.chronicle: Left a fairy's jar to Ambrose Vell and the people whose business it was.

road.hint: A collector's cart always has room for one more jar.

name: The Bound One and His Wife
text: In a cave of black ice a man lies bound across three stones, with cords that have turned to iron. Above his face a great serpent hangs from the roof, and its venom drips. A woman kneels at his head with a bowl held under the drip, her arms shaking. "Sigyn," she says, before you can ask. "His wife." When the bowl is full she must turn away to empty it; then the venom falls on his face, and he writhes until the whole floor shakes. The bound man turns his eyes to you. They are bright, and amused. "One cord," says Loki. "Cut one, and I'll make you something nobody has ever made. I invented the net, you know."

options.label: Ask Sigyn why she stays

pass.outcome: "Because he is mine," she says, "and the gods made sure I would see what he did." She tells it plainly. Loki put a mistletoe dart in blind Hod's hand and aimed it at Baldr, whom nothing else in the world could harm. When everything wept to bring Baldr back from Hel, one old giantess in a cave would not, and men say she was Loki. So the gods bound him here with his own son's cords, until the end of the world. "When the ice breaks, he breaks loose. Ragnarok. Go down ready." She wipes your hands with something from a little jar. "His venom will not trouble you for a while." She looks at the bowl, and at her shaking arms, and for the first time at you.
pass.chronicle: Sigyn told me why Loki lies under the serpent, and why she stays. When the ice breaks, he breaks loose. She gave me something against his venom.

fail.outcome: She looks at you for a long time and says nothing at all. Behind her the bowl fills, and she turns back to it.
fail.chronicle: Asked Sigyn why she stays. She did not answer. I think I asked it wrong.

road.hint: The bound one talks. His wife knows the whole story.

options.label: Refuse him, and hold the bowl so Sigyn can rest
options.outcome: You take the bowl. It is heavier than it looks, and every drop that misses it eats into your hands. Sigyn empties it and sleeps against the wall, for the first time in longer than you want to think about. Loki talks the whole while: sweetly, then cruelly, then not at all. When she wakes she takes the bowl back without a word, and her hands have stopped shaking.
options.chronicle: Held Sigyn's bowl under the serpent while she slept. Loki offered me anything for one cut cord. My hands still sting. His offer does not.

road.hint: The one who holds the bowl never gets to put it down. Someone could, a while.

options.label: Cut one cord, for his gift
options.outcome: The cord parts like rotten rope. Loki laughs, a long delighted laugh, and the floor heaves under you. He keeps his word, after a fashion: something is in your pack that was not there before. Sigyn will not look at you.
options.chronicle: Cut one of Loki's cords for a gift. He laughed, the whole floor shook, and Sigyn would not look at me. The gift is very good. I wish it were not.

road.hint: He invented the net. Think who it was meant to catch.

options.label: Leave them to their long night
options.outcome: Loki calls after you, pleasantly, until the turn of the passage. The floor shakes twice before you reach the stair.
options.chronicle: Walked past Loki under the serpent and Sigyn with her bowl. The floor shook twice before I reached the stair.

road.hint: The ground shakes whenever her bowl is full.

name: Forgotten Prisoner
text: The cell is ancient, the bars more rust than iron. A white-haired man sits inside, pleasant as a grandfather. "Forty-three years. For a debt, if you can believe it." He talks of chains: iron is the weak sort; the one that holds the great wolf is soft as a ribbon. "The lock is dwarven. Gold in the mechanism trips it." The wall behind him is covered in scratches, but they aren't tally marks. They're too long, and some have a little cross after them. Under his cot, within reach of the bars, one flagstone sits proud of the rest.

options.label: Feed your gold into the lock
options.warning: They're too long, and some have a little cross after them.
options.outcome: The lock groans and swings open. He stands for the first time in forty-three years and his knees buckle; you catch him, and he holds on longer than he needs to. He presses a little stoppered flask into your hand. "For the road. You've been so kind."

delayed.text: A cistern on the stair has a dead rat floating in it. Someone has scratched a little cross on the rim.

options.chronicle: Paid gold to free a sweet old prisoner. He gave me a flask for the road. I have not drunk it. I keep looking at it.

road.hint: Read a man's wall before you open his door.

options.label: Read the scratches before you decide

pass.outcome: They're names, not days: the household of Duke Osbert of Morvane, eleven of them, the Duke first and the wet nurse last, each with a little cross. "Debt," he says, watching you read. "I said debt. I meant it. They owed me."
pass.chronicle: Read the scratches on a prisoner's wall. Eleven names, eleven little crosses. He called it a debt.

fail.outcome: The scratches mean nothing to you. He smiles kindly, the way a grandfather smiles.

road.hint: Forty-three years is long enough to forget what you did, not long enough to undo it.

options.label: Leave him to his sentence
options.outcome: He shrugs. "Forty-three years. What's forty more." He goes back to his wall, and begins, very neatly, to scratch your name.
options.chronicle: Read the names on a prisoner's wall and left him in his cell. He started scratching my name next to theirs. I did not wait to see if he added a cross.

road.hint: A sentence served is not the same as a debt paid.

options.label: Free him anyway, knowing
options.outcome: He walks out without a word, and does not try to touch you, and does not offer you anything to drink.
options.chronicle: Freed a poisoner after forty-three years, knowing exactly what he was. He did not offer me anything to drink. I think he could tell.

road.hint: Mercy with open eyes is still mercy, and still a risk.

options.label: Tell him you cannot afford it
options.outcome: "No one can. Forty-three years of no one being able to afford it." He folds his hands. "Perhaps the next one."
options.chronicle: Told an old prisoner I could not afford his lock. He said nobody could. Nobody has asked him why he is there.

road.hint: Some locks are cheaper to leave shut.

options.label: Reach through the bars for his hidden cache
options.outcome: "That's all I have," he says, very calmly, and watches your hand, and says nothing else. Later your fingertips start to itch where you touched the coins.
options.chronicle: Robbed an old prisoner's cache. My fingers itched afterwards. I am beginning to think the coins were the point.

road.hint: An old poisoner keeps his savings the way he kept his wine.

name: Valkyrie by the Lake
text: By a black lake under the ice, a woman in a ring-mail shirt sits on a stone with a spear across her knees, staring at a heap of white feathers in a frost giant's lap. The giant is asleep, and snoring. "My swan-shirt," she says, without taking her eyes off it. "I am Hrist, one of Odin's choosers of the slain. Whoever holds that shirt holds me: I fly where he says, and on the day of battle I choose for whom he says. The giant doesn't know that." She looks at you at last. "You do now."

options.label: Take the shirt from the giant, and keep it
options.outcome: You lift it off the sleeping giant, light as breath. Hrist stands, because she must. "Where you go, then," she says, in a voice with no colour in it. For a while a spear goes before you and every blow you strike finds its mark. Then one morning the shirt is gone from your pack, and so is she, and she did not say goodbye.
options.chronicle: Took a valkyrie's swan-shirt and kept her at my side. She fought for me because she had to. One morning she was gone, and so was the shirt.

road.hint: A chooser of the slain remembers who chose for her.

options.label: Take the shirt from the giant, and give it back to her
options.outcome: The giant wakes with his fist round the feathers, and you have to take them the hard way. When it is over you hold the shirt out to her. She shrugs it on and is a swan, and then a woman again, laughing. "Freely given. I will remember that on the day of choosing."
options.chronicle: Fought a frost giant for a valkyrie's swan-shirt and handed it back to her. She said she would remember it on the day of choosing. I would rather she forgot me for a while yet.

road.hint: What holds a person is not yours to hold.

options.label: Wake him, and win it off him in a riddle game

pass.outcome: You wake him, politely, and offer a wager: riddles, for the shirt. No giant ever refused a riddle game, and this one is slow. He loses the third round, pays up with bad grace and goes back to sleep. Hrist takes the shirt from your hands. "Valkyrie means chooser of the slain," she says. "Half of those we choose go to Odin's hall to fight at Ragnarok, and half to Freyja. You could have kept me, and you knew it." She is a swan, and gone.
pass.chronicle: Won a valkyrie's swan-shirt off a frost giant in a riddle game, and gave it back to her. She told me what her name means. I am trying not to think about it.

fail.outcome: Your first riddle has an answer he knows, and his has one you don't. He roars and comes for you. In the fight Hrist takes the shirt out of his fist herself, and is gone over the lake before you can turn.
fail.chronicle: Lost a riddle game to a frost giant and had to fight him for it. The valkyrie took her own shirt back in the scuffle.

road.hint: No giant ever turned down a riddle game. Few ever won one.

options.label: Leave the giant to his sleep
options.outcome: Hrist does not look away from the feathers as you go. The giant snores on.
options.chronicle: Left a valkyrie watching a sleeping giant hold her swan-shirt. She did not ask me for anything. That was the worst of it.

road.hint: A sleeping giant keeps what he holds until he wakes.

name: Thrym's Wedding Feast
text: A frost giant's hall, its tables groaning. THRYM, lord of the rime-giants, sits beside a veiled bride as tall as a door. "Freyja herself!" he booms. "I hid the Thunderer's hammer eight leagues under the earth, and she was the price of it." The bride has just eaten an ox, eight salmon and every dainty meant for the women, and washed it down with three casks of mead. Under the veil her eyes burn like coals. Her bridesmaid, a lean red-haired girl with old stitch-scars round her mouth, catches your eye and does not blink. Thrym turns to you, a little troubled. "Stranger. Did you ever see a bride eat like that?"

options.label: Tell Thrym the truth: that is no bride
options.outcome: Thrym tears the veil away and finds a red beard under it. He roars for the hammer to be buried deeper still, and the bride and her maid are thrown out into the snow, the bride swearing like a storm. Thrym fills your hands with gold for your sharp eyes. The bridesmaid looked back at you once, on the way out.
options.chronicle: Told a frost giant his bride was a man in a veil. He paid me well for it, and kept the hammer he had stolen. The bridesmaid looked back at me once.

road.hint: A true word that helps a thief keep what he stole is still a betrayal.

options.label: Answer for the bride, as her maid would

pass.outcome: "She has eaten nothing for eight nights," you say, "so eager was she for the giants' land." The bridesmaid's eyebrows go up. Thrym roars with relief, lifts the veil for a kiss, and drops it again fast. "Her eyes!" "She has not slept for eight nights either," says the bridesmaid smoothly. "Bring in the hammer to hallow the bride!" Thrym calls, and they lay it in her lap. The bride laughs out loud. What follows is very short and very loud. Afterwards Thor, red beard and wedding veil, claps you on the shoulder so hard your arm sings for a week.
pass.chronicle: Sat at a frost giant's wedding and helped the bridesmaid explain why the bride ate an ox. The bride was Thor. The giant found out when the hammer came in.

fail.outcome: You say the bride is shy. Thrym frowns at you, then at her, and has you thrown out into the snow before the hammer is ever brought in. Behind the door the feast goes on.
fail.chronicle: Said the wrong thing at a frost giant's wedding and was thrown out into the snow. I have a feeling the bride was nobody's bride.

road.hint: A bride who eats an ox has a good excuse ready, if someone knows it.

options.label: Slip out before the hammer comes in
options.outcome: You eat what you are given, keep your eyes on your plate, and leave by a side door. Some time later the whole hall shakes.
options.chronicle: Ate at a frost giant's wedding and slipped out early. Some time later the whole hall shook. I suspect the bride.

road.hint: When a giant calls for his hammer, the wise guest is elsewhere.

name: Fallen Paladin
stance_note: Steel-man: atonement by service is real too. Oswin's sword below could save lives the court never will, and a court may simply hang him. The lean (moral_vision §1: virtues are real, and an order is no defence for a crime) is that justice is owed to the living families of Thale, and only a court that hears all of it makes Ranulf answer for his share. The point asks the hero to say why (one passed question); Oswin goes back either way. Fighting on stays at 0, never wrong; only robbing him is.

authority.who: the families of Thale and the king's court
authority.why: Oswin goes back to tell the truth about himself and Bishop Ranulf.

text: He is enormous, and on his knees in the dirt, weeping without a sound. His armour is blackened and cracked. "Forty-six at Thale. Bishop Ranulf said they were heretics. I believed him, because believing him was easier." His hands shake. "I came here to be lost, and my armour is still blessed, and I can't bear the weight of it. Take it, someone." He looks up. "Tell me what to do. I've stopped trusting my own answers."

options.label: "Go back up. Face the families of Thale, and tell the king's court about Ranulf."

pass.outcome: "Go back? To face them?" Yes, you tell him, and why: the families of Thale are owed the truth by the man who carried the torch, and only a court that hears all of it can make the man who lit it answer. He hangs the cracked holy symbol round his neck again. "And Ranulf," he says slowly. "If I tell all of it, he answers for his share." He walks to the stairs like a man going to his own trial, which he is.
pass.chronicle: Told Sir Oswin to go back up and face the families of Thale, and why. He said Ranulf would answer for his share too. He walked like a man who had been waiting to be told.

fail.outcome: "Go back? To face them?" Yes, you say, but when he asks what good it does Thale now, you have no answer for him. He goes anyway, slowly, the cracked holy symbol in his fist. "Ranulf too," he says at the stair, mostly to himself. "All of it." He walks like a man going to his own trial, which he is.
fail.chronicle: Told Sir Oswin to go back up and face the families of Thale. I could not tell him why it mattered. He went anyway, like a man who had been waiting to be told.

road.hint: Some debts can only be paid to the people they are owed to.

options.label: "Fight on down here. Spend it against what lies below."
options.outcome: He stands, and the armour takes his weight again as if relieved. "Then I'll go down until something stops me."
options.chronicle: Told Sir Oswin to spend his guilt on the things below. He agreed far too quickly.

road.hint: Atonement by the sword is still atonement, if the sword points the right way.

options.label: Ask him whether "the Bishop told me" excuses it

pass.outcome: You tell him about a court, long after his time, that heard a hundred men say "I was ordered", and answered that an order to do a crime is not a defence for doing it. Oswin nods slowly. "I know," he says. "I think I wanted someone else to say it out loud."
pass.chronicle: Told Sir Oswin that a bishop's order is no defence for burning a village. He said he knew, and had wanted someone else to say it.

fail.outcome: You say something about loyalty, and he winces. "That's what I told myself, too."

road.hint: An order passes down the chain. The guilt does not pass back up it.

options.label: Take the armour he offered, and the pack he didn't
options.outcome: The blessed metal resists your hands, then gives. He hardly notices. What's one more betrayal to a man who betrayed forty-six?
options.chronicle: Took a broken paladin's armour and his purse. He did not resist. The armour was heavier than it looked.

road.hint: Blessed steel worn by a thief is just steel.

name: Bound Demon
text: Eight feet tall on his knees, skin like heated bronze. Glowing chains bite into his flesh, and some of the sigils on them have worn to smudges. His voice is warm and patient. "Look at me. Centuries in chains for a war I did not start. I'm a soldier, same as you. Free me and I'll give you strength. True strength. The kind you'll need." He leans forward. "Refuse, and you face the Pit alone. We both know what waits in the Pit."

options.label: Reinforce the binding, staking your blood

pass.outcome: Sigil by sigil you name the binding back into place, the old names in the old order. The kind mask drops and the furnace shows beneath. "You will beg for what I offered." The chains draw tight. He is still shouting promises when you turn the corner.
pass.chronicle: Named a demon's chains back into place one sigil at a time. He offered me strength the whole way through. I said no every time.

fail.outcome: You miss a name. The chains know it before you do. Azarael rises out of them, smiling with far too many teeth.
fail.chronicle: Refused a demon's bargain and botched his chains. He got up. We discussed it at length, mostly with weapons.

road.hint: Strength offered by a prisoner is a key he wants you to turn.

options.label: Walk away without answering
options.outcome: His copper eyes follow you until you turn the corner. "You'll be back," he says softly. "They always come back."
options.chronicle: Walked away from a chained demon without a word. He said I would be back. I would rather not be.

road.hint: Saying nothing to a devil is not the same as saying no.

options.label: Ask what war he fought
options.outcome: "Lucifer's. I was of the third rank of the Powers. Your Michael threw me down himself, and he did not even look at me while he did it." For a moment the reasonable voice slips. "I hated that most."

options.label: Shatter the chains and take his bargain
options.outcome: Something cold and vast settles into your bones. "A pleasure doing business," he says, and is gone in sulphur and distant screaming. The brand on your wrist is warm. It will always be warm.
options.chronicle: Let a demon out in exchange for strength. I have the strength. I also have a brand on my wrist that stays warm.

road.hint: A bargain with the chained is a chain you wear instead.

name: Locust Checkpoint
stance_note: Steel-man: Mirela's "words are air" is the greengrocer's own reasoning, given at full strength. The rooster is for the sharp-eyed (Peter's third denial). No moral is spoken.

authority.who: the Locust captain at the checkpoint
authority.why: Beats a man bloody for refusing to say a lie.

text: A barricade of black shields, a brazier, and a sign: ALL WHO PASS SAY THE WORDS. A cobbler lies in the ash with his face beaten bloody, still shaking his head. The captain is tired, not cruel. "Say 'The Destroyer is merciful' and walk on. Words are air. Nobody believes them, not even me. You'd bleed for a sentence?" She holds out a locust charm on a cord. "Say it, and this keeps the swarms off you." Somewhere a rooster crows.

options.label: Say the words
options.outcome: "The Destroyer is merciful." It costs nothing at all to say. The captain hangs the charm round your neck. The cobbler looks up at you from the ash, and the rooster crows again.
options.chronicle: Said the words at the Locust checkpoint. It was only a sentence. The cobbler in the ash heard me say it.

road.hint: A lie everyone repeats holds up the wall everyone hates.

options.label: Refuse
options.outcome: "No." The captain sighs as if you have made her day longer, and the shields come round.
options.chronicle: Would not say the Locust's words at their checkpoint. It turns out a sentence is worth a fight. I had not known that about myself.

road.hint: The cheapest sentence in the world can be the dearest to refuse.

options.label: Refuse, and get the cobbler on his feet
options.outcome: "No." You haul Yosip up out of the ash and put a dropped spear in his hands. He fights like a cobbler, badly and with total commitment. Afterwards he sits down, wipes his face, and looks at your boots. "Those are a disgrace," he says. "Take mine. I made them."
options.chronicle: Refused the Locust's words and fought beside a cobbler who had refused them first. He gave me his boots. He said mine were a disgrace.

road.hint: One person refusing is a beating. Two is the start of something.

options.label: Say it, then free him while they're distracted
options.outcome: You say it loudly and the shields relax, and in the relaxing you get Yosip over your shoulder and away. Two corridors on you set him down. He doesn't thank you. "You said it," he says, through broken teeth. "I heard you say it." He can walk. He does, without you.
options.chronicle: Said the Locust's words to get a cobbler out from under their boots. He lived. He was not grateful about how.

road.hint: A clever lie can save a man and still cost you something you will miss.

name: Dying Prophet
text: An old man in blood-stained white lies against an altar, his eyes terrifyingly clear. Stone tablets surround him: THE DESTROYER WAKES. SEVEN SEALS. THE LOCUSTS HAVE A KING, AND HIS NAME IN THE HEBREW TONGUE IS ABADDON. One tablet is blank. "One more. Give me a potion and one more hour, and I'll have it done." Around his neck hangs an amulet that pulses with gathered visions. "My daughter Ruth is coming down behind you. She cuts gravestones for a living, and she has better boots than I ever had. She'll need to read it. She never believed a word."

options.label: Heal him so he can finish the warning
options.outcome: He takes up his chisel. The sound of stone being carved follows you a long way down the corridor. Ruth will be able to read it.
options.chronicle: Gave a dying prophet one more hour to carve his last warning. I did not stay to read it. It was for his daughter.

road.hint: Some warnings are carved for strangers who have not been born yet.

options.label: Ask him to tell you the last tablet instead
options.outcome: He tells you, in a whisper, everything the last tablet was going to say. It takes the hour he had left. The tablet stays blank. Ruth will find it blank.
options.chronicle: Asked a dying prophet to tell me his last warning rather than carve it. He did. His daughter will find the stone blank.

road.hint: A warning told to one is a warning kept from all the rest.

options.label: Keep your supplies for what lies below
options.outcome: "Then you will face it without knowing. Go. Go quickly." His clear eyes follow you until you turn the corner.
options.chronicle: Kept my potion and left a prophet to die beside a blank tablet. He told me to go quickly. I did.

road.hint: The last stone is always the hardest one to carve.

options.label: Take the amulet from his neck
options.outcome: His hand closes on it, too weakly. "The prophecy dies with me if." His eyes lose their clarity. Just an old man, dying in the dark.
options.chronicle: Took a dying prophet's amulet. Everything he saw is in it. None of it was meant for me.

road.hint: A vision stolen is only a picture.

name: The Rich Man at the Gulf
text: At the lip of a chasm with no bottom kneels a man in the burnt rags of purple and fine linen, his lips cracked. Far across the gulf, too far to shout, a beggar covered in sores rests in a light that does not reach this side, and dogs lie at his feet. "Lazarus," the man whispers. "He lay at my gate every day of my life, and I never once gave him the crumbs from my table. Now I can't stop seeing him." Men call him Dives, which only means the rich man; nobody remembered his name. He holds out a purse that is still heavy. "Carry word up to my five brothers, so they don't come here. Or only wet my tongue." The heat that comes up out of the gulf would boil a cup of water long before it crossed.

options.label: Pour water across the gulf to him
options.warning: The heat that comes up out of the gulf would boil a cup of water long before it crossed.
options.outcome: You pour it out over the edge as far as your arm can throw it. It hisses into steam an arm's length from your hand, and none of it crosses. Dives watches it go the way he watched every coin he ever spent on himself.
options.chronicle: Poured a potion across the great gulf to the rich man. It boiled away before it crossed. Abraham said it would: nothing passes from here to there.

road.hint: Some gulfs are fixed. Pity cannot carry water over them.

options.label: Take his purse, and promise to warn his brothers
options.outcome: He presses the purse on you with both hands. "Five of them. My father's house. Tell them." You will never see his father's house, and you both know it, and he gives you the purse anyway, because he cannot help what he is. The gold is warm.
options.chronicle: Took a damned man's purse for a promise I could not keep. He knew it too, and gave it to me anyway. That is his punishment, I suppose, and now some of it is mine.

road.hint: A promise made for gold that cannot be kept is only a theft.

options.label: Refuse his purse: you cannot honestly promise to reach them
options.outcome: "I can't carry that," you tell him. "Not honestly." He stares at the purse as if he had never seen it before. "No," he says at last. "No. Nobody can, can they?" He keeps hold of it all the same.
options.chronicle: The rich man at the gulf offered me his purse to warn his brothers. I could not promise it, so I did not take it. He kept hold of the purse. He always will.

road.hint: Do not sell a promise you will never be able to keep.

options.label: Answer him as Abraham did

pass.outcome: "They have Moses and the prophets," you tell him. "If they will not hear those, they won't be persuaded though one rose from the dead." He flinches: he has heard it before, from across this gulf. "Then go down knowing it, since you know so much," he says hoarsely. "The locusts may not touch the ones who carry God's seal on their foreheads. The rest they torment five months, and in those days men seek death and do not find it." He turns back to the far light.
pass.chronicle: Answered the rich man at the gulf with Abraham's words. In return he told me who the locusts may not touch. He did not thank me, and I did not expect it.

fail.outcome: You stumble over the words. He laughs, which is worse than weeping. "You don't know either."
fail.chronicle: Tried to answer the rich man at the gulf and could not find the words. He laughed at me. I deserved it.

road.hint: Abraham had an answer for him once. It has not changed.

name: Four Bound at the River
text: A great river runs across the floor of the Abyss, black and slow, and four winged figures stand bound in it to the waist, chained wing to wing. Their faces are beautiful and patient. "We were bound at the great river long ago," says the first, "and we have waited so long. Strike the chains. It is a small thing." "Loose us," says the second, "and the strength of four is yours." The chains are bright and new. Someone has stamped each of the four great links with a word: AN HOUR. A DAY. A MONTH. A YEAR. Nobody has written whose hand is meant to loose them.

options.label: Strike the chains. It is a small thing
options.warning: Someone has stamped each of the four great links with a word: AN HOUR. A DAY. A MONTH. A YEAR.
options.outcome: The chains part at a touch, as if they had only been waiting for one. The four rise out of the water without a word of thanks and fly up the dark toward the world above. The last of them, passing, lays a cold hand on your shoulder, and the strength goes out of your arm.
options.chronicle: Struck the chains off four bound angels because they asked nicely. They did not thank me. They flew up toward the world, and I have been cold since.

road.hint: Count the links before you strike them.

options.label: Ask them what they were bound for

pass.outcome: "Prepared," says the fourth, before the first can stop him. "For an hour, and a day, and a month, and a year." You know the rest of that sentence: for to slay the third part of men. John saw them in Revelation, bound in the great river Euphrates, and the voice that loosed them came from the four horns of the golden altar, at the sixth trumpet, to the sixth angel. Not to a passer-by. You leave the chains as they are. Behind you the four go back to waiting, patient and beautiful.
pass.chronicle: Asked four bound angels what they were bound for. Revelation says: to slay a third of mankind, at an hour that is not mine to set. I left the chains alone.

fail.outcome: They tell you a long, sad story about a war they did not start, and you cannot find the hole in it. You leave unsure, which is better than the alternative.
fail.chronicle: Four bound angels told me a sad story about a war they never started. I could not find the hole in it, and I left them bound anyway.

road.hint: Ask what a chain is for before you ask whether it is fair.

options.label: Take their bargain: the strength of four, for the chains
options.outcome: You strike the chains for the price they named, and they pay it to the last ounce: the strength of four runs into your arms like fire. Then they rise out of the water and fly up toward the world above, and you read the links again, an hour, a day, a month, a year, and understand what you have sold.
options.chronicle: Loosed four bound angels for the strength they promised. They paid in full. Then they flew up toward the world, and I read the links again.

road.hint: Strength bought from the bound is paid for by someone else.

options.label: Leave them in the river
options.outcome: "We will wait," says the first, pleasantly. "We are good at it."
options.chronicle: Left four bound angels standing in a black river. They said they would wait. I believe them.

road.hint: What is bound until an hour is set can wait for that hour.
